771.title: Constantinople, 381
771.hook: the council completes the Creed on the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life
771.carry: the lord and giver of life
771.howItsDone: Catholics say the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed at Sunday Mass and may begin prayer or work with Come, Holy Spirit; the Spirit is invoked at every baptism and confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the date of Easter: Nicaea hoped the whole Church would keep the resurrection on one day. Your line was one day, someday. Which date did you put on a calendar, and with whom? Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Read the creed of Nicaea to the end and something is missing. It spends line after line on the Son: God of God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father. Then it reaches the Holy Spirit and says only: and in the Holy Spirit. For a while that was enough. Then some teachers began to say the Spirit was less than God: a power God uses, a holy servant, but not Lord. So the bishops gathered again, this time in the emperor's new capital on the water. Today, the council that finished the sentence. Today, Constantinople.
screen: `NICAEA, ON THE SON: LINE AFTER LINE.` → `ON THE SPIRIT: ONE LINE.` → `THE SENTENCE UNFINISHED.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says the faith about the Spirit was confessed at the second ecumenical council, at Constantinople, in 381, and that the creed said at Mass comes from these first two councils together. So the creed called the Nicene Creed is really Nicaea, finished at Constantinople. Here is what the bishops added. The old Book of Common Prayer gives its opening words like this: "And I believe in the Holy Ghost, The Lord and giver of life." Then, in the council's words as the Catechism summarizes them: who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who has spoken through the prophets. Take the two titles one at a time. Lord. That's the same title the creed gives the Son. Not a force, not an energy, not an errand runner. Lord. And worshiped together with the Father and the Son, which the creed would never say of a creature. Then, giver of life. That reaches back to the first pages of Genesis, where God shapes the man from the earth and "breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." The Church hears the Spirit in that breath, and Catholics say the one who gave life in the beginning gives life now: in baptism, in prayer, in a dry heart that starts to move again. As the Church tells it, the bishops didn't invent a new teaching. They said out loud what the Church already did when it baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. In the Church's telling: three names, one God, and the third is not an afterthought.
screen: `NICAEA, FINISHED AT CONSTANTINOPLE.` · `LORD: NOT A FORCE.` · `THE BREATH OF LIFE IN GENESIS.` · then, large: `THE LORD AND GIVER OF LIFE.` · then: `THE THIRD NAME, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let your breath carry today's line. Settle, and breathe slowly. Notice that this breath came without your deciding, and the next one is already on its way. On the in-breath, the Lord. On the out-breath, and giver of life. If you pray, you can use the short traditional prayer, Come, Holy Spirit, and then just stay quiet. If you don't, let the breath itself be enough to notice for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Constantinople. The city of the second ecumenical council, where the creed was finished with the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life. Today's word.
Your line: the lord and giver of life. Today, when something in you or around you comes back to life, a plant, a friendship, your own energy, say the line. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: Ephesus, 431
772.hook: Mary is God-bearer; the Church of the East and Rome signed a shared statement on Christ in 1994
772.howItsDone: Catholics call Mary the Mother of God in the Hail Mary and keep the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God on the first of January; the 1994 common declaration with the Assyrian Church of the East is part of the Church's ecumenical dialogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople: the council that finished the creed with the Holy Spirit. Your line was the lord and giver of life. What came back to life around you, and did you say the line? Day seven hundred seventy-two.

"And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" That's Elizabeth in Luke's Gospel, greeting her cousin Mary at the door. The mother of my Lord. Christians in the East came to call Mary by a Greek title, Theotokos, the God-bearer, the one who gave birth to God. Then a bishop of Constantinople, Nestorius, objected. Call her the mother of Christ, he said; don't say she bore God. It sounds like a quarrel about Mary. It was really a quarrel about her son. The bishops who answered it met in a city called Ephesus.
screen: `THE MOTHER OF MY LORD.` → `THEOTOKOS, THE GOD-BEARER.` → `NESTORIUS OBJECTS.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says the Council of Ephesus proclaimed in 431 that Mary truly became the Mother of God, by the human conception of the Son of God in her womb. And it names what the council was guarding against: the idea that Christ was a human person joined to the divine person of God's Son, two someones sharing one body. Ephesus said no. The child Mary carried was not a man God later moved into. He was God the Son, become man in her. So when Catholics call Mary Mother of God, they are first saying something about Jesus: the one she held in her arms is the same one through whom all things were made. It's the same title said in the Hail Mary: Holy Mary, Mother of God. There is a second half to this story. One family of Christians, the Assyrian Church of the East, did not accept the council's decisions, and the two churches went separate ways. Then in 1994 Pope John Paul II and the Catholicos-Patriarch of the Church of the East, Mar Dinkha the Fourth, signed a common statement on Christ. In it they say they confess the same faith in Christ, truly God and truly man, one person. They note the Church of the East prays to Mary as the Mother of Christ our God and Savior, and the Catholic Church calls her the Mother of God and also the Mother of Christ, and each recognizes the other's words as expressing the same faith. A quarrel healed later. Not everything between them is settled. But two churches found, on the question of who Christ is, that they had been saying the same thing in different words.
screen: `MOTHER OF GOD: A WORD ABOUT JESUS.` · `NOT TWO SOMEONES, ONE PERSON.` · `TWO CHURCHES, SEPARATE WAYS.` · then, large: `A COMMON STATEMENT ON CHRIST.` · then: `THE SAME FAITH, DIFFERENT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the Church of the East in mind. Settle, and breathe. Its Christians pray in an ancient Syriac tradition. You may never have met one; that's fine. Hold them anyway. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the unity their leaders and the popes have been walking toward. If you don't, just wish them peace for a few breaths. Then, if there's an old quarrel of your own that turned out to be about words more than substance, let it sit beside them. The bell holds the time.
Ephesus. The council that called Mary Mother of God, Theotokos, to say that her son is one person, truly God. Today's word.
Your line: a quarrel healed later. Today, look again at one old disagreement and ask whether you and the other person were saying the same thing in different words. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

773.title: Chalcedon, 451
773.hook: one person in two natures; the Oriental Orthodox did not accept it, and recent dialogues found more agreement than feared
773.howItsDone: Catholics confess Chalcedon's teaching in the Creed's 'true God from true God' and 'became man'; the Catholic Church holds official dialogues with the Oriental Orthodox churches, and popes have signed common declarations with Coptic and Armenian patriarchs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephesus: Mary the God-bearer, and a statement signed with the Church of the East. Your line was a quarrel healed later. Did an old disagreement turn out to be about words? Day seven hundred seventy-three.

Bethany, outside a tomb. A man named Lazarus has been dead four days. His sisters are grieving, the neighbors are weeping, and John's Gospel says, in three short words: "And Jesus wept." Real tears, from a real friend. A few verses later, the same man stands at the same tomb and calls out, "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man walks out. One person. Tears in one moment, a voice that empties a grave in the next. How do you say who that is? Bishops meeting at Chalcedon tried to put it into words.
screen: `A TOMB IN BETHANY.` → `AND JESUS WEPT.` → `LAZARUS, COME FORTH.`

segments.voice: Ephesus had said Christ is one person. The next question was how his divinity and his humanity belong together in that one person. Did the human dissolve into the divine, like a drop of honey in the sea? Or were there really two, side by side? The Catechism gives Chalcedon's answer, from 451: one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division or separation. Four withouts. Without confusion: the human isn't swallowed by the divine. Without change: neither stops being what it is. Without division, without separation: there aren't two Christs. So the one who wept at the tomb and the one who called Lazarus out are not two people taking turns. Two natures, one Christ. Now the hard part of this story. A family of ancient churches did not accept Chalcedon's wording: among them the Coptic Church of Egypt, the Armenian Apostolic Church, and the Syriac and Ethiopian Orthodox churches. Together they are called the Oriental Orthodox churches. They preferred to speak, with Cyril of Alexandria, of one nature of the Word made flesh, and they heard in two natures a risk of splitting Christ in two. Chalcedon's defenders heard in one nature a risk of swallowing his humanity. Each side, some historians say, feared the worst of the other. Then in our own time popes have signed common declarations with Coptic and Armenian patriarchs, saying together that Christ is perfect God and perfect man, one Christ. The old formulas still differ. The agreement underneath turned out larger than either side feared.
screen: `ONE PERSON. HOW DO THE TWO BELONG?` · `FOUR WITHOUTS.` · then, large: `TWO NATURES, ONE CHRIST.` · then: `CHURCHES THAT KEPT OTHER WORDS.` · `MORE AGREEMENT THAN FEARED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Coptic and Armenian Christians in mind. Sit back, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind a Coptic church, an Armenian church, or simply the people who worship in them, wherever they are today. They pray to the same Christ who wept at Lazarus's tomb. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for full communion between their churches and Rome. If you don't, just hold them with good will. Then let the Bethany story run once more, slowly: the tears, and then the voice at the tomb. The bell holds the time.
Chalcedon. The council that confessed Christ as one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion and without separation. Today's word.
Your line: two natures, one christ. Today, when you hear someone's tears and someone's strength in the same voice, let it remind you of the tomb in Bethany. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

774.title: Constantinople III, 681
774.hook: Christ has a truly human will as well as a divine one
774.howItsDone: Catholics pray Thy will be done in the Our Father and meditate on Christ's prayer in Gethsemane in the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chalcedon: one person, truly God and truly man, the one who wept at the tomb and called Lazarus out. Your line was two natures, one christ. Where did you hear tears and strength in one voice? Day seven hundred seventy-four.

A garden at night, across the valley from Jerusalem. Jesus has gone a little apart from his friends, and Luke's Gospel says he kneels and prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Read it slowly. There is a will that would rather the cup pass. And there is a yes. Long afterward, bishops were arguing over that one sentence, because it holds a question: when Jesus says my will, whose will is that? The answer came from the council called Constantinople the Third.
screen: `A GARDEN AT NIGHT.` → `REMOVE THIS CHALICE FROM ME.` → `WHOSE WILL IS THAT?`

segments.voice: After Chalcedon said Christ has two natures, some tried a middle road to bring divided churches back together. Fine, they said, two natures, but only one will: the divine will doing all the willing, the humanity just carried along. It sounded peaceful. Others saw the cost. A monk remembered as Maximus the Confessor argued that a human nature without a human will isn't fully human. Gregory of Nazianzus had put the principle long before: what Christ did not take on, he did not heal. Tradition says he paid dearly for saying so. The Catechism gives the council's answer. At the sixth ecumenical council, Constantinople III, in 681, the Church confessed that Christ has two wills and two natural operations, divine and human. And here's the key: they are not opposed. His human will does not resist his divine will. It follows it, submits to it. Now go back to the garden. Not my will, but thine. As the council's defenders saw it, if Jesus had no human will, there would be nothing to surrender, and those words would be play-acting. Because he does, the garden is real. A real human wanting, a real dread of the cup, and a real human yes, given freely to the Father. That's the council's claim. On this reading, Christ knows from inside what it costs a person to say yes when everything in them leans the other way, and the yes is not a script but a choice made by someone with a will like ours. A human will. Not crushed, not erased, but given.
screen: `ONE WILL: A MIDDLE ROAD.` · `MAXIMUS: NOT FULLY HUMAN WITHOUT IT.` · `TWO WILLS, NOT OPPOSED.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.` · then: `A REAL YES, FREELY GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your own will. Sit still for a moment, hands in your lap. Bring to mind one thing you want today that you may not get: a result, an apology, an easy afternoon. Don't pretend you don't want it. Name it honestly, the way the garden prayer does. Then see if there's any room, even a little, to open your hands around it. Not to stop wanting. Just to loosen your grip. If you pray, you can say Jesus's words from the garden, not my will, but thine be done. If you don't, simply breathe out with open hands. The bell holds the time.
Constantinople III. The sixth ecumenical council, which confessed that Christ has a truly human will as well as a divine one, never opposed. Today's word.
Your line: a human will. Today, the next time you're about to dig in, pause long enough to choose, instead of just pushing. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

775.title: Nicaea II, 787
775.hook: images are venerated, not worshiped; the honor passes to the one shown
775.howItsDone: Catholics venerate images by bowing, kneeling, lighting candles or kissing a crucifix or icon, as on Good Friday when the faithful come forward to venerate the cross; the Church teaches that adoration is given to God alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople III: Christ has a truly human will, and in the garden it said yes. Your line was a human will. Where did you pause to choose instead of digging in? Day seven hundred seventy-five.

An old photograph, soft at the corners, of a grandmother who has died. Her grandson takes it out of a drawer before a long trip, looks at it a moment, and kisses it. Then he puts it back. No one watching would say he kissed paper. The kiss went somewhere. It went to her. Hold that small, ordinary gesture, because a council of bishops built a careful distinction on almost exactly that. Today, a council that drew a line between two kinds of honor, and a word for one of them: veneration.
screen: `AN OLD PHOTOGRAPH.` → `A KISS BEFORE A TRIP.` → `THE KISS WENT TO HER.`

segments.voice: Earlier this year, this path met John of Damascus, who defended icons when emperors were tearing them down. The argument went on, and the bishops met again at Nicaea. The Catechism says the seventh ecumenical council, at Nicaea in 787, justified the veneration of icons, of Christ, of the Mother of God, of the angels and all the saints, on the basis of the mystery of the Word made flesh. Now the line it drew. There is worship, adoration, which belongs to God alone. And there is veneration: respect, honor, a bow, a kiss, a candle. Catholics give an icon or a statue veneration, never worship. The Catechism quotes Saint Basil to explain why it isn't idolatry: the honor rendered to an image passes to its prototype, to the one it shows. And the council itself adds: whoever venerates an image venerates the person portrayed in it. Like the kiss on the photograph. It doesn't stop at the paper. It passes through. Why does the Incarnation matter here? Because the council rested its case on it. John's Gospel says, "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." John of Damascus had started his defense there; the council made that starting point the whole Church's. Notice how much hangs on this: the council's whole defense of images rests on one distinction, between worship and honor. Lose it and either the icons go, or God gets crowded out. Keep it, and the honor passes through.
screen: `THE SEVENTH COUNCIL, AT NICAEA.` · `WORSHIP FOR GOD; HONOR FOR IMAGES.` · then, large: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.` · then: `THE HONOR PASSES TO THE ONE SHOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give honor that passes through. If you have an icon, a crucifix, a statue or a holy card nearby, bring it close. If you don't, a photograph of someone you love will do. Look at it for a while, and breathe. Notice where your attention goes: past the wood and paint, to the one it shows. Then, if it fits you, bow your head to it, or kiss it, the way people kiss icons in church. If you pray, let the gesture be your prayer, without words. If you don't, let it simply be thanks. The bell holds the time.
Veneration. Honor given to an image or a saint, never the worship that belongs to God; the honor passes to the one shown. Today's word.
Your line: honor passes through. Today, when you thank someone for a gift, let the thanks go past the thing to the person behind it. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

776.hook: East and West separate over authority and the Creed; in 1965 pope and patriarch lifted the old excommunications
776.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January, and popes and ecumenical patriarchs have met, prayed together and signed common declarations since the excommunications were lifted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicaea II and veneration: the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows. Your line was honor passes through. Whose gift did you thank, past the thing itself? Day seven hundred seventy-six.

"That there be no schisms among you." Saint Paul wrote that to a church in Corinth that was splitting into camps: I am of Paul, I am of Apollo. A schism is a tear. Not a disagreement, which a family can live with, but a tear in the fabric, where people who belong at one table stop sitting at it together. Paul begged that church not to tear. Long after, a tear came between two churches, East and West. Today, the year that stands for it, and the word for what happened: schism.
screen: `NO SCHISMS AMONG YOU.` → `A TEAR, NOT A DISAGREEMENT.` → `TWO CHURCHES, ONE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Two questions had been pulling the Latin West and the Greek East apart. The first was authority: what the bishop of Rome's role is among all the bishops. Catholics hold that the pope, as Peter's successor, has a primacy over the whole Church. Orthodox Christians honor Rome's place among the ancient churches but understand that primacy differently. The second was the Creed. In the West, the line about the Spirit came to read who proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Catechism says plainly that and the Son was not in the creed confessed at Constantinople, and that the Eastern tradition stresses the Father as the first origin of the Spirit, while the Latin tradition stresses the communion of Father and Son. Then came the moment the year stands for. The common declaration that Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras made in 1965 recalls it: in 1054, legates of the Roman see pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the Patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, and the patriarch and his synod answered with one of their own. In time it hardened into a lasting break. Now the healing. In that same declaration, the pope and the patriarch said they regretted the offensive words and gestures on both sides, and they removed the old excommunications from the memory and the midst of the Church. That didn't end the schism. The two churches are still not in full communion. But the curses are gone, and the two churches keep talking. A wound, still healing. And under all of it, Jesus's own prayer in John: "That they all may be one."
screen: `AUTHORITY: THE POPE'S ROLE.` · `THE CREED: AND THE SON.` · `A SENTENCE, AND AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · then: `THE OLD CURSES, REMOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Orthodox Christians in mind. Let your breathing slow on its own. Bring to mind an Orthodox church you've passed, a Greek or Russian or Romanian or Ukrainian neighbor, or simply the Orthodox Christians of the world at prayer today. They say the creed of Nicaea and Constantinople. They venerate the icons Nicaea defended. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the day both churches share one table. If you don't, just wish them well, and stay with that wish for the whole sit. The bell holds the time.
Schism. A tear in the Church's unity, where people who belong at one table stop sharing it. Today's word.
Your line: a wound, still healing. Today, take back one harsh word you said in an old quarrel, even if the quarrel itself isn't settled. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

777.hook: crusaders sack Christian Constantinople; centuries later a pope expresses sorrow
777.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox leaders have met, prayed together and asked forgiveness for past wrongs; Catholics who seek reconciliation often bring an old wrong to confession and then make amends where they can.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the schism: East and West pulling apart. Your line was a wound, still healing. This week ran from Constantinople and Ephesus through Chalcedon and the icons to that break. Today the wound is cut deeper. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

The army had taken the cross. It set out, in its own telling, to reach the Holy Land. Instead, the ships ended up under the walls of Constantinople, the great Christian city of the East, and the soldiers broke in. Churches were stripped. Altars were looted. Christians from the West plundered Christians of the East, in the name of a holy war. Today's word is a year, the one in the title: twelve oh four. And today's story has two ends, one at those walls and one in Athens, a very long time afterward.
screen: `THE ARMY TOOK THE CROSS.` → `THE WRONG CITY.` → `TWO ENDS TO ONE STORY.`

segments.voice: Start with what happened. Crusaders from the West were drawn into a fight over the throne of the Eastern empire. It ended with the city sacked by people baptized into the same faith in Christ as its citizens. Next, what Rome said at the time. Pope Innocent the Third had forbidden attacks on Christians, and when he heard what was done, he wrote in anger. In a letter, he said that the Greek Church now had reason to see in the Latins only an example of ruin and the works of darkness. He did not pretend it was a victory. Then, what it did. Before, the schism could feel like a matter of bishops and letters. After the sack, it was memory: families, churches, a city. In the East, the wound now had a face. Finally, the other end. Centuries later, Pope John Paul the Second stood in Athens before the Orthodox Archbishop and named the sack of Constantinople out loud. He said it was tragic that men who set out for the Holy Land turned against their own brothers in the faith, and that it filled Catholics with deep regret. He asked the Lord's forgiveness for wrongs done by Catholics to Orthodox Christians. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, that if your brother has something against you, leave your gift at the altar, and "go first to be reconciled to thy brother." That's today's line: sorrow, centuries later. Late is not the same as never.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say sorry for an old wrong. Let one come to mind, something you did a long time ago that you never named. It doesn't need to be large. Stay with it for the sit. Don't argue your side. Just name, quietly, what you did and who it touched. If you pray, you can bring it before God and ask for the grace to say it. If the person can still be reached, you might decide, before the bell ends, when and how you'll tell them. The bell holds the time.
